title: Everything Starts with This
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder follows up a post on burnout with the claim that the binding constraint on a business is not its systems but the operator behind them. She describes years of building processes from what she calls an outdated internal operating system — panic, perfectionism and proving — and argues that those systems were optimised for survival rather than scale without her noticing. Reading Benjamin Hardy's The Science of Scaling gives her the organising idea: set a goal unreasonable enough that it forces you to become the person who could achieve it, because identity functions as the ceiling on performance. The move the piece makes is to invert the usual founder instinct: instead of installing a better CRM, fixing the funnel or hiring the team, upgrade the decision-maker first, since a system built by an un-upgraded self will keep breaking. She offers three diagnostic questions — whether a behaviour aligns with the future self or the fear-based self, whether the week is structured like that of someone building a $100M company, and what would be deleted if only needle-moving work survived. Her conclusion is subtractive: clarity comes from eliminating what doesn't align rather than optimising everything. Short, personal, and useful mainly as a framing device for leaders whose operating model has outgrown its author.
points: Mulder's diagnosis is that most founders debug the system while leaving the operator untouched, which is why the fixes keep failing.
The 'optimising for survival, not scale' distinction is the sharpest idea in the piece — systems inherit the emotional state of whoever designed them.
She converts Hardy's identity argument into a weekly test: does this behaviour belong to the future self or the fear-based self?
The prescribed action is deletion rather than optimisation — strip everything that doesn't move the stretch goal instead of improving it.
Useful caution for leaders scaling from a mess: the mindset that produced the mess cannot be the one that clears it.
quotes: In my last post, I shared how burnout doesn’t always come from broken systems. It comes from running your life and business through an outdated operating system: in my case, panic, perfectionism, proving.

Hardy talks about setting a goal so unreasonable it forces you to become the version of yourself who could achieve it. And that clicked. Because for years, I built my systems from the version of me that was overwhelmed, reactive, and still trying to prove herself.
I was optimizing for survival, not scale. And I didn’t even realize it.
All while still making decisions from a version of themselves that’s stuck in the past. If the you behind the system hasn’t upgraded, the system itself will always break.
This isn’t manifesting. It’s mechanics. It’s the science of who you’re becoming.
The big ‘ah ha’? Trying to scale from the mindset that built the mess doesn’t fix the mess.
